transforms.name: content-to-iocs
transforms.description: Extracts common indicators of compromise from Document content
transforms.long_description: Scans the text of a Document entity, taking the content property and falling back to the entity value, and pulls out indicators of compromise. If the optional iocsearcher library is installed it is used as the extraction backend; otherwise the transform falls back to built-in regular expressions for URLs, email addresses, IPv4 addresses, MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, and domain names. Each distinct indicator becomes an entity linked back to the source Document: URL, Domain, and EmailAddress with a mentions edge, IPAddress with a resolves to edge, and Hash with a contains hash edge. Values are deduplicated case-insensitively and every output records that it was extracted from document content. The transform makes no network calls and works purely on text already on the graph, and it reports which backend was used in its run messages.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this once you already have page or report text on the graph, most often the Document produced by URL to Content, and you want that prose turned into pivotable indicator entities. It is the mining half of that chain: URL to Content extracts the readable text, Content to IOCs harvests the indicators from it. Once indicators land on the graph, pivot with WHOIS Lookup or Domain to IP Address for domains, IP to Shodan Host for addresses, and Hash to abuse.ch Malware Intel for file hashes.
transforms.limitations: Extraction is pattern based, so false positives are common. The domain pattern also matches file names such as index.html or setup.exe, the IPv4 pattern matches version strings and other dotted quads that are not addresses, and the hash pattern matches any 32, 40, or 64 character hex string, including git commit IDs, asset fingerprints, and session tokens. Review results before treating them as indicators. Nothing is validated against a threat feed, defanged indicators such as hxxp:// or 1[.]2[.]3[.]4 are not refanged, and coverage depends on how much text the upstream extraction captured.
example_use_cases: Turn a fetched threat report or blog post into pivotable indicator entities
Harvest domains, IPs, and hashes from page text captured by URL to Content
Pull contact addresses and linked URLs out of a scraped page for further pivoting
transforms.author: OGI Team

transforms.name: document-to-phone-numbers
transforms.description: Extracts observed phone numbers from document content, normalizes them when possible, and preserves source context
transforms.long_description: Reads the content property of a Document entity, or the entity value when no content is stored, and extracts phone numbers from the text. When the phonenumbers library is available its matcher drives detection and accepted numbers are normalized to E.164 using the configured default region; a conservative regex fallback catches candidates the library misses and normalizes them by digit count. Each accepted number becomes a PhoneNumber entity joined to the Document by an observed phone edge, carrying a confidence score, the raw matched text, the normalized form, which normalization method produced it, a context snippet of configurable width taken from the surrounding text, and the document URL when one is present. Candidates are sorted by confidence and deduplicated, and output stops at max_results, 20 by default and 200 at most, so the weakest matches are the ones dropped. The transform is offline and makes no requests.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this on a Document already on the graph, typically the page text captured by URL to Content, when you want contact numbers from a directory page, a staff listing, a PDF, or a scraped profile. It pairs with Content to IOCs, which mines the same document for network indicators. If you are working from a Person entity and want numbers pulled from that person's attached profile URLs and biography, with scoring based on how close each number sits to the name, use Person to Phone Numbers instead.
transforms.limitations: Digit sequences that look like phone numbers are extracted whether or not they are phone numbers: order and invoice numbers, tax and registration IDs, dates, and product codes all reach the regex fallback, which is why every result carries a confidence score and a context snippet for review. Results beyond the max_results cap are discarded after confidence sorting. Without the phonenumbers library installed only the weaker fallback runs, and its normalization assumes the configured region. The transform attributes nothing: a number in a document is not evidence that any person or organization owns it.
example_use_cases: Extract contact numbers from a company staff directory page captured as a Document
Pull phone numbers out of a scraped PDF or report already stored on the graph
Build a contact list from the text of a conference or speaker page

transforms.name: domain-to-urls
transforms.description: Fetches robots.txt and extracts URLs from Sitemap and Disallow directives
transforms.long_description: Fetches robots.txt over https from the input domain, following redirects, and parses the file for Sitemap and Disallow directives. Sitemap values are taken as absolute URLs, while Disallow paths are joined to the domain to form a full https URL. Comments, blank lines, and a bare disallow of the site root are skipped. Each distinct result becomes a URL entity recording that it came from robots.txt, linked to the input Domain by a hosts edge. Output is capped at 50 URLs by default, and the run messages report both the total number found and the fact that the list was truncated. Only the robots.txt file itself is retrieved: referenced sitemaps are emitted as URLs but never downloaded or expanded, and no page is rendered in a browser.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this early against a domain to find paths the site owner would rather keep out of search results: admin panels, staging areas, internal tools, and export endpoints often appear in Disallow lines. It is a cheap single-request way to build a starting list of URLs for a web target. Feed the results into URL to HTTP Headers to fingerprint the server, URL to Outbound Links to widen coverage, or URL to Content to capture the page text, which Content to IOCs can then mine for indicators.
transforms.limitations: Output is capped at 50 URLs, so large robots.txt files are truncated. Only https is attempted with no http fallback, and any response other than HTTP 200 yields nothing. Disallow entries are used verbatim, so wildcard patterns such as /admin/* or /*.php$ become URL entities that do not resolve to real pages. Many sites publish no robots.txt or list only trivial paths. Sitemap URLs are emitted but never fetched, so the pages they list are not discovered. TLS certificate verification is disabled for the request.
example_use_cases: Discover admin, staging, and export paths a site explicitly hides from crawlers
Collect sitemap locations for a target domain before deeper enumeration
Build a starting URL list for a web target with a single low-noise request
transforms.author: OGI Team

transforms.name: person-to-phone-numbers
transforms.description: Finds public phone numbers associated with a person from attached text, documents, and profile URLs with proximity-based scoring
transforms.long_description: Works only from context already attached to the Person entity: the bio, description, and notes properties, embedded document text, and URLs listed under profile, website, links, and document URL properties. Candidate URLs are filtered to those whose path contains part of the person's name or, when include_generic_contact_pages is enabled, a contact-like segment such as contact, team, staff, or about. Those pages are fetched over plain HTTP, restricted to text content types, with localhost and private addresses blocked, then reduced to text by stripping scripts, styles, and tags. Phone candidates come from the phonenumbers library plus a regex fallback and are normalized to E.164. Each candidate is scored: proximity between the number and the person's name raises confidence, a nearby title, role, or employer term raises it further, and a number with no name anywhere near it is penalized. Candidates below min_confidence are discarded and the rest become PhoneNumber entities linked by a possible phone edge, carrying the confidence, the matched name, the proximity distance, a context snippet, the source URL or document label, and a short rationale. The number of sources inspected and results emitted are capped by max_sources and max_results.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this when a Person entity already carries profile URLs, a biography, or attached documents and you want the numbers most plausibly tied to that individual rather than every number on a page. The proximity scoring is what separates it from flat extraction. Run Person to Emails alongside it for the rest of the contact picture. If you want every number in one specific page or file with no attribution scoring, fetch the page with URL to Content and run Document to Phone Numbers on the resulting Document.
transforms.limitations: The transform discovers nothing on its own: a Person entity with no attached URLs, bio, or documents produces no results. Pages are fetched without a browser, so profiles rendered by JavaScript, behind logins, or behind bot protection yield no usable text. Proximity is not ownership, and a switchboard or shared office number sitting near a name on a contact page will score well while still not belonging to that person. The regex fallback also catches reference and ID numbers that merely look like phone numbers. At most max_sources sources are inspected and max_results numbers returned.
example_use_cases: Find a likely direct number for a named executive from their company bio page
Corroborate a phone number already linked to a person against their public profiles
Extract contact details for a person from documents already attached to their entity

transforms.name: url-to-abusech-ioc
transforms.description: Looks up a URL in abuse.ch ThreatFox and maps related IOC context
transforms.long_description: Sends an exact-match IOC search for the URL to the abuse.ch ThreatFox API, keeps the records whose IOC type is url, and uses the first one returned. The input URL entity is enriched in place with that record: threat type and description, malware family, confidence level, reporter, first and last seen dates, reference, tags, and a link to the ThreatFox entry. A Document holding a readable summary of those fields is attached by a has evidence edge. The host of the reported IOC is emitted as an IPAddress or a Domain with a hosted on edge, and every md5, sha1, sha256, or sha3-384 hash on the record, including those on associated malware samples, becomes a Hash entity with an associated sample edge. An abuse.ch Auth-Key is required and is declared under api_keys_required as ABUSECH_API_KEY. The request timeout is configurable between 5 and 30 seconds, and invalid keys or rate limiting are surfaced as run messages.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this when a URL is suspected of hosting malware or acting as command and control infrastructure and you want a community threat feed's view of it, including which malware family it is tied to. It works best on full URLs taken from samples, logs, or reports rather than on site homepages. Pivot from the emitted hashes with Hash to abuse.ch Malware Intel, from the emitted host with Domain to abuse.ch IOCs or IP to Shodan Host, and run URL to urlscan Lookup to see what the page actually rendered.
transforms.limitations: The lookup is an exact match, so a different scheme, a trailing slash, or a changed query string will miss a record that exists for the canonical form. Only the first url-type record is used, so additional ThreatFox entries for the same URL are ignored. ThreatFox is community submitted, so the absence of a record is not evidence that a URL is safe, and the data reflects when it was reported rather than the current state of the URL. An abuse.ch Auth-Key is required and the API enforces rate limits.
example_use_cases: Check whether a URL from a phishing email is a known malware distribution point
Attribute a suspicious URL to a malware family and pull associated sample hashes
Confirm that infrastructure seen in logs is already reported to a public threat feed

transforms.name: url-to-content
transforms.description: Fetches a URL via Playwright and extracts readable text content into a Document entity
transforms.long_description: Launches a headless Chromium browser through Playwright, navigates to the URL, and waits for the network to go idle, so pages that build themselves with JavaScript are captured as rendered rather than as raw source. The final page HTML has script and style blocks and all tags stripped, HTML entities unescaped, and whitespace collapsed, and the result is truncated to max_content_chars, 12000 by default and 200000 at most. The output is a single Document entity linked by a has content edge, named after the page title or the final hostname, carrying the final URL after redirects, the extracted text, the content type, the title, and the character count. Only http and https URLs are accepted, responses of HTTP 400 or above are refused, non-text content types are rejected, and localhost and private network targets are blocked unless allow_local_network is enabled.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this as the first step whenever you need the actual words on a page rather than its metadata, and especially for single-page applications and other JavaScript-heavy sites where a plain HTTP fetch returns an empty shell. It is the front half of the standard chain: URL to Content extracts the readable text into a Document, and Content to IOCs then mines that text for domains, addresses, and hashes. Run Document to Phone Numbers on the same Document for contact numbers, or URL to Outbound Links when you want the page's link graph instead of its text.
transforms.limitations: Playwright and a Chromium browser binary must be installed, and rendering each page is far slower and heavier than a plain fetch. Text is truncated at max_content_chars, so long pages lose their tail. Extraction strips tags rather than identifying the main article, so navigation, footers, and cookie banners end up in the text. Sites behind logins, captchas, or bot protection return the block or consent page, and its text is stored as though it were the real content. Pages that never reach network idle fail on the 20 second navigation timeout.
example_use_cases: Capture the readable text of a threat report before mining it with Content to IOCs
Extract content from a JavaScript-rendered page that a plain HTTP fetch cannot read
Archive the wording of a suspicious landing page as evidence on the graph

transforms.name: url-to-headers
transforms.description: Performs a HEAD request and extracts interesting HTTP headers from a URL
transforms.long_description: Issues a single HTTP HEAD request to the URL, following redirects, and inspects the response for a fixed list of ten headers: Server, X-Powered-By, Content-Type, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-XSS-Protection, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and Set-Cookie. Every one of those that is present becomes an HTTPHeader entity valued as the header name followed by its value, linked to the input URL by a has header edge, with the header name, the header value, and the response status code stored as properties. The status code and each captured header are also reported as run messages. No page body is downloaded and no browser is launched, which makes this one of the cheapest checks available against a live host.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this for a quick technology and security-posture read on a live URL: which server or framework banner is exposed, whether HSTS and a content security policy are configured, and whether cookies are being set. It is a natural follow-up to URLs discovered by Domain to URLs (robots.txt) or URL to Outbound Links, and a cheap way to confirm a host responds before spending a browser render on URL to Content.
transforms.limitations: Only the ten listed headers are captured and everything else in the response is discarded. The request is HEAD only, so servers that reject or mishandle HEAD return nothing, and headers a site sets only on GET responses are never seen. Redirects are followed, so the headers describe the final destination rather than the URL submitted. Values often come from a CDN or reverse proxy and say nothing about the origin server, and banners such as Server and X-Powered-By are trivially spoofed or suppressed. TLS certificate verification is disabled for the request.
example_use_cases: Fingerprint the server and framework behind a URL without downloading the page
Check whether a site sets HSTS, CSP, and clickjacking protections
Confirm a URL is live and see its status code before running heavier transforms
transforms.author: OGI Team

transforms.name: url-to-links
transforms.description: Fetches a page and extracts outbound links and their domains
transforms.long_description: Fetches the page over plain HTTP with a browser-like user agent, following redirects, and scans the raw HTML with a regular expression for anchor tag href attributes. Fragment-only links and mailto, tel, and javascript targets are skipped, and relative hrefs are resolved against the final URL after redirects, so redirected pages still produce correct absolute links. Each distinct http or https link becomes a URL entity recording the source page and linked to the input URL by a links to edge, and each distinct hostname among those links is emitted as a Domain entity recording where it was discovered. Link collection stops at 100 URLs by default, and the run messages report how many links were extracted. Only the one page is fetched; the transform never follows the links it finds and no browser rendering takes place.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this to map where a page points: outbound partners, third-party services, social profiles, and neighbouring pages on the same site. It is a good breadth-first move after landing on a homepage or on paths discovered by Domain to URLs (robots.txt). Follow up with WHOIS Lookup or Domain to IP Address on the emitted domains, and use URL to Content when you want the page's text rather than its link graph, since that text is what Content to IOCs then mines for indicators.
transforms.limitations: The page is fetched, not rendered, so links inserted by JavaScript, loaded on scroll, or built client-side are invisible; for a single-page application this transform will often return almost nothing. Parsing is a regular expression over anchor tags, so URLs in scripts, JSON blobs, iframes, and link elements are missed. Collection stops at 100 links, which truncates link-heavy pages. Emitted Domain entities are created without edges back to the source URL. TLS certificate verification is disabled for the request.
example_use_cases: Map the outbound relationships and third-party services referenced by a landing page
Discover social media profiles and partner sites linked from a company homepage
Expand a single known URL into neighbouring pages and domains for further pivoting
transforms.author: OGI Team

transforms.name: url-to-urlscan-lookup
transforms.description: Looks up the most recent matching urlscan result for a URL
transforms.long_description: Queries the urlscan.io search API for existing scans of the URL, asking for a single result with a query that matches the value against both the submitted task URL and the final page URL. When a scan is found the input URL entity is enriched in place; no new entities and no edges are created. The added properties cover the urlscan result identifier and report link, the task and page URLs, the page domain, IP address, country, server banner, and HTTP status, plus the scan visibility, the scan date, and the number of distinct domains contacted when urlscan reports it. Run messages surface the report link and the headline page details. A urlscan API key is required and is declared under api_keys_required as URLSCAN_API_KEY. The request timeout is configurable between 5 and 60 seconds, and invalid keys or rate limiting are surfaced as run messages.
transforms.when_to_use: Use this when you want to know whether a URL has already been scanned publicly and what it looked like at the time, without visiting it yourself or announcing your interest to the host. That makes it a safe opening move on phishing and malware URLs. Follow it with URL to abuse.ch IOC to check the URL against a malware feed, and with URL to Content if you decide you need the current page text, which Content to IOCs can then mine for indicators.
transforms.limitations: This searches the existing urlscan index and never submits a new scan, so a URL nobody has scanned returns nothing. Matching is on the exact URL string, so a differing query string, trailing slash, or scheme will miss a scan of the canonical form. Only the single most recent result is kept and older scans are ignored. The data describes the page as it was when scanned, which may be long out of date. A urlscan API key is required and the API enforces rate limits.
example_use_cases: Check what a suspicious URL rendered as without visiting it yourself
Find the IP address and hosting country behind a phishing URL from an existing scan
Confirm a URL has been publicly reported and scanned before escalating
transforms.author: OGI Team
